question: Recent journalistic investigations have revealed that AI-generated YouTube and Instagram accounts that have millions of followers and have been verified by Meta pretend to be real doctors or healers and spread health disinformation. A high percentage of those accounts also promote supplements, despite the fact that in Spain it is illegal to advertise products ‘with a purported health purpose ...

that purport to have testimonials from health professionals’. The Digital Services Act requires large platforms to mitigate the risks of illegal content being disseminated and harm being done to public health via their services. In light of the above: 1.

Has the Commission assessed whether the existence of such AI-generated accounts reveals potential shortcomings in the risk mitigation measures that very large online platforms are required to implement to mitigate potential negative effects on public health, as provided for in Articles 34 and 35 of the Digital Services Act? 2.

Does the Commission intend to initiate additional investigations or take further enforcement action when platforms verify, through paid subscriptions such as Meta Verified, AI-generated profiles that do not represent real people? 3.

Has the Commission considered asking Amazon for information about its Associates Program and the systemic risks this could pose with regard to the financing of creators who spread health disinformation?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (26.10.2026) The Digital Services Act (DSA)1 obliges providers of very large online platforms and very large online search engines to annually identify, assess and analyse the systemic risks stemming from their services, including risks to public health. The creation and dissemination of AI-generated accounts on social media should be considered in the risk assessments, e.g.

when employed for manipulating the service. The risks of manipulation by AI-generated content, including accounts, may affect the protection of public health. The Commission has already issued guidance recognising the specific risks associated with AIgenerated content. The DSA Election Guidelines2 recommend that providers clearly label generative AI content in a manner easily recognised by users.

The voluntary Code of Conduct on Disinformation3 includes strong measures to address the spread of disinformation, including dissemination of AI-generated content. Enforcing the DSA is a priority for the Commission. For example, the Commission is currently investigating Meta's Facebook and Instagram for potential DSA breaches, particularly regarding the dissemination of deceptive advertisement and disinformation4.

In addition, under the AI Act5 providers must implement machine-readable marking for AIgenerated content. Labelling obligations apply to deep fakes and to AI-generated/manipulated content, if intended to inform on matters of public interest.

The Commission is currently assessing Amazon’s 2026 Risk Assessment under the DSA, including the section ‘Public Health Risk’ where Amazon assesses risks related to the dissemination of health disinformation, and the measures in place in case of illegal content posted by an influencer under the Associates Program.
1 Regulation (EU) 2022/2065 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 19 October 2022 on a Single

Market for Digital Services and amending Directive 2000/31/EC (Digital Services Act) (Text with EEA relevance); OJ L 277, 27.10.2022, ELI: http://data.europa.eu/eli/reg/2022/2065/oj. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A52024XC03014&qid=1714466886277. 3 https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/library/code-conduct-disinformation. 4 https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/ip_24_2373. 5 Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/reg/2024/1689/oj/eng.
